summary: Gives rules for downgrading X.400 1988 messages to the older 1984 form when they carry MIME content types. It replaces chapter 6 of RFC 1328 and leaves the rest of that document in place. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A fancy new gadget must sometimes work with an older machine. This memo says how to turn a modern message into a plainer one the old machine can read.

questions: how to convert x.400 88 messages to x.400 84
what is mime encapsulation in x.400
subtitle: Converting modern MIME email to an older email system format.

tldr.problem: X.400(88) and the older X.400(84) systems handle email differently, making it difficult to exchange messages between them when MIME content types are involved.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1496 specifies conversion rules that translate X.400(88) messages with MIME content into X.400(84) format by converting extended body parts to basic forms and encapsulating incompatible content in IA5Text body parts with MIME headers.
tldr.outcome: The standard enables interworking between X.400(84) and modern MIME-based email systems, allowing older X.400(84) users to receive and handle multimedia content.

today: RFC 1496 is marked Historic. It served an important role in the 1990s for organizations still using X.400(84) systems that needed to receive MIME-based messages. Modern systems now primarily use SMTP and MIME directly, making this translation layer largely obsolete.

sections.title: Bridging Two Email Protocol Versions
sections.content:
X.400 is an international standard for electronic mail that went through several versions. RFC 1496 addresses the challenge of translating messages between X.400(88) and the older X.400(84) standard when the messages contain MIME content types.

The document updates RFC 1328 (which covered X.400(88) to X.400(84) downgrading) by specifying how to handle modern MIME content that X.400(84) does not natively support, allowing systems to interwork despite their version differences.
sections.plainLanguage: Old and new email systems speak slightly different languages. This explains how to translate a fancy new message so an old system can read it.

sections.title: The Three-Step Conversion Strategy
sections.content:
The approach defines three principles for downgrading messages. First, convert what you can: X.400(88) features that have equivalents in X.400(84) should be translated directly. Second, encapsulate what you must: content that X.400(84) cannot handle is wrapped in a special format. Third, never drop a message: every message must arrive intact, even if some formatting is lost.

Messages traveling between SMTP(MIME) and X.400(84) systems take an intermediate path through X.400(88), preventing direct incompatible conversions.
sections.plainLanguage: Convert what works, wrap what doesn't, never lose anything. Messages always take the same safe route through a middle version that understands both sides.

sections.title: Conversion and Encapsulation Rules
sections.content:
For X.400(88) body parts that have both basic and extended forms, the gateway transforms extended forms to basic forms by combining parameters and data into a single sequence, allowing X.400(88) systems using extended forms to communicate with X.400(84) systems.

For content that cannot be represented in X.400(84), an IA5Text body part is created starting with MIME headers (MIME-Version, Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding) followed by the encoded content. In the reverse direction, IA5 body parts beginning with MIME-Version are converted according to MIME rules before being included in X.400(88) messages.
sections.plainLanguage: If the old system understands something, just send it normally. If not, wrap it up with MIME labels on the outside so it can be unwrapped later.
